title: Function Notation & Graph Characteristics
learningObjective: FN2: Use and interpret function notation to evaluate a function for a given input value and find a corresponding input value given an output value. FN3: Use the graph of a function to find the domain and range in interval notation, the x- and y-intercepts, the maxima and minima, and where it is increasing and decreasing using interval notation.

faqs.question: What is function notation, and why do we use f(x) instead of y?
faqs.answer: Function notation replaces y with a label that tells you which function and which input you're using. Writing f(x) instead of y does two things: it names the function (so you can tell f(x) apart from g(x) if you're using more than one), and it keeps the input value visible right in the notation. Once you get comfortable with it, f(x) actually gives you more information than y does.

faqs.question: What does f(x) actually mean?
faqs.answer:
f(x) means "the output of function f when the input is x." It's not f times x — there's no multiplication happening. Think of f as a machine: you feed in a value for x, and f(x) is whatever comes out.
Worked Example

Let \( f(x) = 2x + 3 \)

To find \( f(5) \), replace every \( x \) with \( 5 \):

\( f(5) = 2(5) + 3 = 10 + 3 = 13 \)

So the input \( 5 \) produces the output \( 13 \).

faqs.question: What's the difference between evaluating f(a) and solving f(x) = a?
faqs.answer:
These are opposite directions. Evaluating f(a) means you know the input and you're finding the output — plug in a, simplify, get a number. Solving f(x) = a means you know the output and you're finding the input — you're working backward to figure out which x-value(s) produce that result. Same function, opposite question.
Worked Example

Let \( f(x) = 2x + 3 \)

Evaluate \( f(4) \): plug in \( x=4 \) → \( f(4)=2(4)+3=11 \)

Solve \( f(x) = 11 \): set \( 2x+3=11 \), so \( x = 4 \)

Same fact, asked two different ways.

On the FN2 CheckIt exercise, the "solve" direction comes with a graph, not a formula: see the FAQ "How is solving f(x) = value different when I'm given a graph versus an equation?" Solving from a formula is class and homework practice.

faqs.question: What is the domain and range of a graph, and how is that different from finding domain algebraically (like we did in FN1)?
faqs.answer:
The idea is the same — domain is still every possible input, range is still every possible output — but the method changes. In FN1, you found domain by looking at an equation and identifying restrictions (square roots, denominators). Here, you're reading the domain directly off the graph itself: how far left-to-right does the graph stretch (domain), and how far bottom-to-top does it stretch (range)?

The bar under the x-axis, labeled Domain, runs from x = −2 to x = 6: the left-right spread of the graph. The bar labeled Range runs from y = 1 to y = 7: its up-down spread. Both ends have filled dots, so both intervals use brackets.

faqs.question: What does it mean for a function to be increasing or decreasing?
faqs.answer: A function is increasing where the y-values go up as the x-values go up — reading the graph left to right, it's climbing. It's decreasing where the y-values go down as x increases — the graph is falling. These are always described using x-values (the interval on the x-axis), not y-values. A change in steepness alone (a corner where the graph keeps going up, just more steeply) does not change increasing to decreasing.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a local max/min and a global max/min?
faqs.answer:
A global max is the greatest y-value the graph reaches anywhere; a global min is the least. A graph has at most one global max value and one global min value (or none, if it never actually reaches a highest or lowest height), though the same value can occur at more than one point. A local max or min is a "hilltop" or "valley": a point on the graph that is higher (or lower) than all the points near it on both sides, even if it isn't the highest or lowest overall. A graph can have several local maxes and mins. In this course, an endpoint of a graph is never counted as a local max or min, but a filled endpoint can be the global max or min.

The point (1, 6) is the highest point on the whole graph, so the global max is 6; it is also a local max. The point (4, −3) is the lowest, so the global min is −3; it is also a local min. (−4, 3) and (−2, 1) are only local: the graph goes higher and lower elsewhere.

faqs.question: How do I evaluate something like f(x + h) when the input is an expression, not a number?
faqs.answer:
Extension: inputs like x + h go beyond the FN2 CheckIt exercise (you'll use them again in calculus). Same process as evaluating f(5) — you're still just plugging the input in for every x in the function's rule. The only difference is your input is now an expression instead of a number, so you substitute (x + h) everywhere you see x, then simplify using algebra (often expanding a binomial or distributing).
Worked Example

Let \( f(x) = x^2 + 3x \). Find \( f(x+h) \).

Replace every \( x \) with \( (x+h) \):

\( f(x+h) = (x+h)^2 + 3(x+h) \)

\( = x^2 + 2xh + h^2 + 3x + 3h \)

faqs.question: How do I know which piece to use in a piecewise function?
faqs.answer: Find the x-value you're evaluating, then check which interval condition it satisfies. Go through the pieces one at a time and ask: "does my x-value fit this piece's condition?" Once you find the interval that matches, use only that piece's equation — ignore the others completely. Exactly one piece's condition includes the boundary value; the ≤ or ≥ tells you which.

faqs.question: How do I read domain and range directly off a graph, in interval notation?
faqs.answer:
For domain, scan left to right: where does the graph start and where does it stop? For range, scan bottom to top: what are the lowest and highest heights the graph reaches? The top or bottom of the range can come from a turning point or from an end of the graph, so check both. At an end, a filled dot means that value is included (bracket [ ]) and an open dot means it is not (parenthesis ( )). An arrow means the graph keeps going forever, so that side uses ∞ or −∞, which always gets a parenthesis.

The graph starts at a filled dot at x = −1 (included, bracket) and stops at an open dot at x = 7 (not included, parenthesis): the domain is [−1, 7). The lowest height is 1, at the filled dot, and the graph rises toward 7 without reaching it: the range is [1, 7).

faqs.question: Why can a function have several x-intercepts but at most one y-intercept?
faqs.answer: This connects back to the definition of a function from FN1: each input has exactly one output. Several x-intercepts just means several different x-values share the same output, 0, and different inputs are allowed to share an output. But two different y-intercepts would mean the input x = 0 has two different outputs, which breaks the rule, so the graph would not be a function. A function can also have no y-intercept at all, if 0 is not in its domain.

faqs.question: How do I find increasing/decreasing intervals from a graph?
faqs.answer:
Trace the graph with your finger from left to right. Wherever your finger moves up, the function is increasing; wherever it moves down, it is decreasing. Write the intervals with x-values only. In this course and on CheckIt, these intervals always use parentheses at both ends: at turning points, and at the ends of the graph too, even where the dot is filled. If the graph has an arrow, that side uses ∞ or −∞.

The graph rises until x = 2, then falls, and the arrows show it keeps going in both directions: increasing on (−∞, 2) and decreasing on (2, ∞).

faqs.question: How do I tell a local minimum from a global minimum on a graph?
faqs.answer: Ask yourself: is this point lower than the points just around it (local), or is it the lowest point on the whole graph (global)? A global minimum that sits at a valley is also a local minimum. But in this course an endpoint is never counted as a local minimum, so a global minimum at a filled endpoint is global only. And a local minimum isn't always the global one: there might be a lower point somewhere else on the graph. On CheckIt, a global minimum is given as a y-value (for example, "global minimum of −4") and a local minimum as a point.

faqs.question: What happens if a graph doesn't have a global max or min at all?
faqs.answer:
A graph has no global maximum when it never actually reaches a highest height. On CheckIt this happens at an open dot: if the open dot at one end of the graph is higher than every point the graph does reach, the graph gets as close to that height as you like but never gets there, so no point is highest. (It also happens when an arrow shows the graph rising forever.) In that case, write "no global maximum." The same goes for a global minimum with an open dot (or arrow) at the bottom. An open dot that is partway up doesn't matter: if some turning point or filled end is higher, that is the global max. Don't force a number where one doesn't exist.

The open dot at (5, 6) is higher than every point on the graph, but it is not part of the graph, so there is no global maximum; the range is [−1, 6). The lowest point, (−2, −1), is reached, so the global minimum is −1.

faqs.question: How is solving f(x) = value different when I'm given a graph versus an equation?
faqs.answer:
With an equation, you solve algebraically. With a graph, you're looking for where the height of the graph (the y-value) equals the target value: draw the horizontal line at that height and find every point where it meets the graph, including points where it just touches the graph and an end of the graph with a filled dot (an open dot doesn't count). Each meeting point gives one x-value answer, so there can be no answers, one, or several.

The dashed line y = 2 meets the graph three times, at x = −3, x = 0 and x = 3, so f(x) = 2 has three solutions.

faqs.question: How does function notation (FN2) connect back to what we learned about functions in FN1?
faqs.answer: FN1 taught you how to recognize whether something is a function and how to find its domain and range. FN2 gives you the language to actually work with functions once you've identified them. f(x) is just a more powerful way of writing the y you were already using — everything about domain, inputs, and outputs still applies, just with clearer notation.

faqs.question: Why does understanding a graph's behavior (FN3) matter for what's coming later in the course?
faqs.answer: Reading graphs — intercepts, domain, range, increasing/decreasing, max/min — is a skill you'll use constantly for the rest of precalculus and into calculus. Every new family of functions you study (polynomial, rational, exponential, trigonometric) will ask you to describe its graph using these exact same tools. This section is building a vocabulary you'll rely on all semester.

guided.title: Grade a Classmate's Piecewise Work
guided.prompt: I'm practicing FN2 in Math 172: evaluating a two-piece function defined on -5 < x < 5. Make up one piecewise function like the ones on my CheckIt exercise. Use two different kinds of piece from this list: a polynomial a*x^2 + b*x or a*x^3 + b (a = 1, 2, or 3; b a whole number from -3 to 3); a square root sqrt(a*x^2 + b) with a = 1 or 3 and b = 1 or 5; or a fraction (a*x + b)/(c*x^2 + d) with a = 1 or 4, b a whole number from -4 to 4, c = 1 or 2, and d a whole number from 1 to 5. Split the two pieces at a whole number from -2 to 2, and put "or equal to" on exactly one side of the split. Then show me a classmate's work finding the function's value at one whole number left of the split, one whole number right of it, and at the split itself, with exact answers (simplified square roots and reduced fractions). Put exactly one deliberate mistake in the work: the wrong piece at the split, a sign error with a negative input, or a square root or fraction left unsimplified. Don't tell me which line it's in. For each line, I'll say which piece the input belongs to and why, then find the mistake and fix it. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Input or Output? Read the Notation
guided.prompt: I'm learning function notation in Math 172 (FN2). Ask me one question at a time, mixing these four kinds: (1) a statement like h(-2) = 7, where I say which number is the input, which is the output, and what point is on the graph; (2) a sentence in context, like D(30) = 12, where D(t) is how many miles a bus has traveled t minutes after leaving the station, which I explain in words with units; (3) evaluating a formula like f(x) = 3x - 4 at a negative input; (4) the reverse: finding the x with f(x) = a given number, for a linear formula like that one. Before each answer, I'll say whether I'm being given the input or the output. Don't confirm until I explain my choice. On the fourth question, show me your own answer first with one deliberate mistake in it (for example, swapping the input and output, or plugging the given output in for x) and ask me to find it. (On my CheckIt exercise the reverse question comes with a graph instead of a formula, so I'll also tell you how I'd answer it from a graph.) After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Read a Graph from a Point List
guided.prompt: I'm practicing FN3 in Math 172: reading every feature of a graph. You can't show me a picture, so describe a graph as a list: where it starts (its x and y, and whether the dot there is filled or open), every point where it turns around, every point where it crosses the x-axis, where it crosses the y-axis, and where it ends (filled or open dot). Use whole numbers from -10 to 10, make it one unbroken curve with three turning points, and make sure it only turns around at the points you list. I'll sketch it on paper. Then I'll find the domain, range, x- and y-intercepts, local maxima and minima (as points), the global maximum and minimum (as y-values, or "none"), and the intervals where it increases and decreases. I'll write intervals the way my CheckIt exercise does: x-values, with parentheses for increasing and decreasing even at a filled dot. In my course, an endpoint is never a local max or min, but a filled endpoint can be the global one. After I answer, show me your own answer key with one deliberate mistake in it, and I'll find it by checking each feature against my sketch. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Local or Global? Endpoints and Open Dots
guided.prompt: I'm learning the difference between local and global maxima and minima (FN3). My notes say: an endpoint of a graph is never a local max or min; a filled endpoint can be the global max or min; and an open dot is never reached, so it can't be either. Describe three graphs to me, one at a time, as a list of points: where it starts and ends (filled or open dot) and each turning point, with whole-number coordinates. Graph 1: a filled endpoint that is higher than every turning point. Graph 2: an open dot at one end that is lower than every point the graph reaches. Graph 3: an open dot partway up, with a turning point higher than it. For each graph, I'll name the local maxima and minima as points and give the global maximum and minimum as y-values or "none", and explain why. Don't confirm until I explain. For Graph 3, give your own answer first, with one deliberate mistake for me to find. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Connect FN2 and FN3 to the Bigger Picture
guided.prompt: I just learned function notation (evaluating functions, piecewise functions) and how to read key features from a graph (intercepts, domain, range, increasing/decreasing, local and global extrema). Can you explain how these two skills work together, and give me one example of a real-world function where reading its graph tells a meaningful story?

paths.label: FN2: Function Notation
paths.intro: Builds to the FN2 check: evaluating functions from formulas, piecewise definitions, and graphs. Practice scope: the path practices both parts of the FN2 CheckIt exercise: evaluating a two-piece function on \(-5 < x < 5\) (polynomial, square-root, or fraction pieces) at a point on each side of the split and at the split itself, with exact answers; and reading a graph made of straight segments to find \(g(c)\) and every \(x\) with \(g(x) = b\). The optional Stretch in "Find every input from an output" (solving from a formula) goes beyond the FN2 CheckIt exercise.

stages.desc: Two quick skills this section leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Substitute a negative number
stops.target: Substitute a negative number into an expression and simplify using order of operations.
stops.mistake: Writing -3^2 = -9 instead of (-3)^2 = 9, or losing the sign in -4(-3).
stops.reflect: Why do parentheses matter when you substitute a negative number?

stops.title: Read an inequality
stops.target: Decide whether a number belongs to an interval like \(-5 < x \le 2\), paying attention to \(<\) versus \(\le\).
stops.cold: Which of these numbers satisfy \(-5 < x \le 2\)? \(\;-5,\; 0,\; 2,\; 3\)
stops.coldPlain: Which of these numbers satisfy -5 < x <= 2 ?  -5, 0, 2, 3
stops.coldA: \(0\) and \(2\). The \(\le\) includes \(2\); the \(<\) leaves out \(-5\); \(3\) is too big.
stops.solution: -5 < x <= 2 means x is bigger than -5 (not equal) and at most 2 (equal is allowed). So 0 and 2 work; -5 fails because the left sign is strict; 3 is too big.
stops.mistake: Treating < and <= as the same, especially at the endpoints.
stops.again: Which of these numbers satisfy \(1 \le x < 5\)? \(\;0,\; 1,\; 4.5,\; 5\)
stops.againA: \(1\) and \(4.5\). The \(\le\) includes \(1\); the \(<\) leaves out \(5\).
stops.reflect: In your own words, what is the difference between \(<\) and \(\le\) at an endpoint?

stages.desc: One stop per skill on the FN2 check, in order.

stops.title: Read function notation
stops.target: Explain what \(f(a) = b\) means: \(a\) is the input, \(b\) is the output, and \((a, b)\) is a point on the graph.
stops.cold: If \(f(4) = 10\), what is the input, what is the output, and what point is on the graph of \(f\)?
stops.coldPlain: If f(4) = 10, what is the input, what is the output, and what point is on the graph of f?
stops.coldA: Input \(4\), output \(10\), point \((4, 10)\). The number inside the parentheses is always the input.
stops.solution: In f(4) = 10, the input is 4 (inside the parentheses) and the output is 10. The point on the graph is (4, 10). f(4) does not mean f times 4.
stops.mistake: Reading f(4) as "f times 4," or swapping input and output when writing the point.
stops.again: You know \(g(-4) = 6\) and \(g(6) = -4\). Write the two points on the graph of \(g\).
stops.againA: \((-4, 6)\) and \((6, -4)\). Input first, output second, so these are two different points.
stops.reflect: How can you tell which number is the input just by looking at the notation?

stops.title: Evaluate from a formula
stops.target: Find \(f(a)\) by replacing every \(x\) in the formula with \(a\), including formulas with square roots and fractions.
stops.mistake: Replacing only some of the x's, or dropping the parentheses around -2.
stops.reflect: What is the one move you make every time, no matter what the formula looks like?

stops.title: Evaluate a piecewise function
stops.target: Evaluate a piecewise function by first deciding which piece the input belongs to, especially at the boundary.
stops.cold:
Let \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 + 3x & -5 < x \le 2 \\ \sqrt{3x^2 + 1} & 2 < x < 5 \end{cases}\)
Find \(f(-3)\), \(f(2)\), and \(f(3)\). Give exact answers.
stops.coldPlain: Let f(x) be piecewise: f(x) = x^2 + 3x when -5 < x <= 2, and f(x) = sqrt(3x^2 + 1) when 2 < x < 5. Find f(-3), f(2), and f(3). Give exact answers.
stops.coldA: \(f(-3) = 9 - 9 = 0\) (top piece). \(f(2) = 4 + 6 = 10\) (top piece, because of the \(\le\)). \(f(3) = \sqrt{27 + 1} = \sqrt{28} = 2\sqrt{7}\) (bottom piece).
stops.solution: Step 1 is always: which piece? -3 is in -5 < x <= 2, so f(-3) = (-3)^2 + 3(-3) = 9 - 9 = 0. 2 is also in -5 < x <= 2 (the <= includes 2), so f(2) = 2^2 + 3(2) = 4 + 6 = 10. 3 is in 2 < x < 5, so f(3) = sqrt(3(9) + 1) = sqrt(28) = sqrt(4 * 7) = 2 sqrt(7).
stops.mistake: Using the wrong piece at the boundary x = 2 (that gives sqrt(13)), writing (-3)^2 as -9, or leaving sqrt(28) unsimplified.
stops.againA: \(g(-3) = \dfrac{-13}{10} = -\dfrac{13}{10}\) (top piece). \(g(-2) = 8 + 2 = 10\) (bottom piece, because the \(\le\) is there). \(g(1) = 2 - 1 = 1\) (bottom piece).
stops.reflect: At a boundary value, how do you decide which piece to use?

stops.title: Find an output from a graph
stops.target: Find \(g(a)\) from a graph: go to \(x = a\), move up or down to the graph, and read the \(y\)-value.
stops.cold: Use the graph of \(g\) to find \(g(-4)\).[[graph:A]]On CheckIt, the ends of the graph won't be marked with dots: the graph just stops, and an end counts when it's inside the interval in the question.
stops.coldPlain: Use the graph of g to find g(-4).
stops.graphNote: The graph of g is made of straight line segments connecting the points (-6, -2), (-3, 4), (1, 0), (4, 6), (6, 4), and it only exists on the interval [-6, 6].
stops.coldA: \(2\). Start at \(x = -4\) on the \(x\)-axis, move up to the graph, and read across: \(y = 2\).
stops.solution: Go to x = -4, move vertically to the graph, and read the height: the segment from (-6, -2) to (-3, 4) rises 2 for every 1 to the right, so at x = -4 the height is -2 + 2(2) = 2. g(-4) = 2.
stops.mistake: Starting on the y-axis at -4 instead of the x-axis.
stops.again: Use the same graph to find \(g(3)\), \(g(0)\), and \(g(1)\).[[graph:A]]
stops.againA: \(g(3) = 4\), \(g(0) = 1\), and \(g(1) = 0\). At \(x = 1\) the graph has a corner on the \(x\)-axis; a corner is a point of the graph like any other.
stops.reflect: Which axis do you start on when you are given the input?

stops.title: Find every input from an output
stops.target: Given an output \(b\), find every \(x\) with \(g(x) = b\): draw the horizontal line \(y = b\) and read each crossing.
stops.coldPlain: For which x-value(s) in the interval [-6, 6] does g(x) = 4?
stops.graphNote: The graph of g is made of straight line segments connecting the points (-6, -2), (-3, 4), (1, 0), (4, 6), (6, 4), and it only exists on the interval [-6, 6].
stops.coldA: \(x = -3,\; 3,\; 6\). The line \(y = 4\) touches the graph three times. Don't forget the endpoint at \(x = 6\).
stops.solution: Draw the horizontal line y = 4 and find every place it meets the graph: at the peak (-3, 4), on the rising segment at (3, 4), and at the right endpoint (6, 4). So x = -3, 3, 6.
stops.mistake: Stopping after the first answer, or reading 4 on the x-axis and finding g(4) instead.
stops.again: For which \(x\)-value(s) in \([-6, 6]\) does \(g(x) = 1\)? (b) For which \(x\)-value(s) in \([-6, 6]\) does \(g(x) = 6\)?[[graph:A]]
stops.againA: \(x = -4.5,\; 0,\; 1.5\). Answers don't have to be whole numbers: each segment has slope \(\pm1\) or \(\pm2\), so crossings can land halfway between grid lines. (b) \(x = 4\) only. The line \(y = 6\) touches the graph only at the peak \((4, 6)\): one answer is possible too.
stops.stretch: Extension (beyond the FN2 CheckIt exercise, which asks this from a graph): without a graph, let \(h(x) = 5x + 7\). Find \(x\) so that \(h(x) = -8\).
stops.reflect: How is "find \(g(4)\)" different from "find \(x\) so that \(g(x) = 4\)"?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same format as the FN2 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Evaluate a piecewise function and read a graph both ways, the way the FN2 check asks.
stops.cold:
Part A. Let \(p(x) = \begin{cases} 2x^2 - 3 & -5 < x < 1 \\ \sqrt{3x^2 + 1} & 1 \le x < 5 \end{cases}\)
Find \(p(-3)\), \(p(1)\), and \(p(2)\).

Part B. Let \(h(x)\) be the function graphed below. Find \(h(1)\). For which \(x\)-value(s) in \([-5, 5]\) does \(h(x) = 3\)?[[graph:B]]
stops.coldPlain: Part A: p(x) = 2x^2 - 3 when -5 < x < 1, and p(x) = sqrt(3x^2 + 1) when 1 <= x < 5. Find p(-3), p(1), p(2). Part B: using the graph of h, find h(1), and find every x in [-5, 5] with h(x) = 3.
stops.graphNote: The graph of h is made of straight line segments connecting the points (-5, 3), (-2, -3), (0, -1), (3, 5), (5, 1), and it only exists on the interval [-5, 5].
stops.solution: A: -3 is in -5 < x < 1, so p(-3) = 2(9) - 3 = 15. 1 is in 1 <= x < 5, so p(1) = sqrt(3 + 1) = 2. 2 is also in 1 <= x < 5, so p(2) = sqrt(12 + 1) = sqrt(13), which is already simplified. B: h(1) = 1 (on the segment from (0, -1) to (3, 5)). The line y = 3 meets the graph at the left endpoint (-5, 3), at (2, 3), and at (4, 3), so x = -5, 2, 4.
stops.mistake: Using the wrong piece at x = 1 (that gives -1), missing an endpoint answer, or mixing up "find h(1)" with "find x where h(x) = 3".
stops.again:
Part A. Let \(q(x) = \begin{cases} x^3 - 2x & -5 < x \le 0 \\ \dfrac{x + 2}{x^2 + 1} & 0 < x < 5 \end{cases}\)
Find \(q(-2)\), \(q(0)\), and \(q(3)\).

Part B. Use the graph of \(g\) from earlier. Find \(g(-1)\). For which \(x\)-value(s) in \([-6, 6]\) does \(g(x) = 5\)?[[graph:A]]
stops.againA:
A. \(q(-2) = -8 + 4 = -4\), \(q(0) = 0\), \(q(3) = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
B. \(g(-1) = 2\). \(g(x) = 5\) when \(x = 3.5\) and \(x = 5\). (The left segment tops out at \(4\), so it never reaches \(5\).)
stops.reflect: Which part of the check do you want to practice more before the real one?

paths.label: FN3: Graph Characteristics
paths.intro: Builds to the FN3 check: reading domain, range, intercepts, extrema, and increasing/decreasing intervals from a graph, and sketching a graph that meets a list of criteria. Practice scope: the path practices both parts of the FN3 CheckIt exercise, with CheckIt's answer forms: intervals of \(x\)-values, with parentheses for increasing and decreasing even at a filled end; intercepts and local maxima and minima as points; and a global maximum or minimum as a \(y\)-value, or "none" when the graph only approaches it at an open dot.

stages.desc: Two quick skills FN3 leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Write interval notation
stops.target: Translate between inequalities and interval notation: parentheses for "not included" (and for \(\infty\)), brackets for "included."
stops.cold: Write each in interval notation: (a) \(-2 < x \le 5\) (b) \(x \ge 3\)
stops.coldPlain: Write each in interval notation: (a) -2 < x <= 5, (b) x >= 3.
stops.coldA: (a) \((-2, 5]\) (b) \([3, \infty)\). Infinity always gets a parenthesis, because you can never reach it.
stops.solution: (a) -2 is not included, so use a parenthesis; 5 is included, so use a bracket: (-2, 5]. (b) 3 is included and there is no upper limit: [3, infinity). Infinity always gets a parenthesis.
stops.mistake: Putting a bracket next to infinity, or flipping which side gets the bracket.
stops.again: (a) Write \([-4, 1)\) as an inequality. (b) Write \(x < 0\) in interval notation.
stops.reflect: How do you decide between a bracket and a parenthesis?

stops.title: Open and closed dots
stops.target: Read whether a graph includes its endpoints: a closed (filled) dot is included, an open (hollow) dot is not.
stops.cold: The graph below is a line segment. Is the point \((2, 4)\) on the graph? Write the \(x\)-values the graph covers in interval notation.[[graph:S1]]
stops.coldPlain: A line segment graph is shown. Is the point (2, 4) on the graph? Write the x-values the graph covers in interval notation.
stops.graphNote: The graph is a straight line segment from a closed dot at (-3, 1) to an open dot at (2, 4).
stops.coldA: No, the open dot means \((2, 4)\) is not included. The \(x\)-values are \([-3, 2)\).
stops.solution: The dot at (2, 4) is open, so that point is not on the graph. The dot at (-3, 1) is closed, so it is included. The x-values run from -3 (included) to 2 (not included): [-3, 2).
stops.mistake: Treating an open dot like a closed one, or reading y-values when the question asks for x-values.
stops.again: For this segment, write the \(x\)-values it covers and the \(y\)-values it covers, both in interval notation.[[graph:S2]]
stops.reflect: What does an open dot at the end of a graph tell you?

stages.desc: One stop per feature on the FN3 check. The first four use the same graph, so you can focus on one feature at a time.

stops.title: Domain and range
stops.target: Find the domain (all \(x\)-values used) and range (all \(y\)-values reached) from a graph, in interval notation.
stops.cold: Find the domain and range of \(f\).[[graph:C]]
stops.coldPlain: Using the graph of f, find the domain and range in interval notation.
stops.graphNote: It is a smooth curve that starts at (-7, 3) with a closed dot and ends at (6, 6) with an open dot. In order, it passes through (-5, 0), (-3, -4), (-1, 0), (0, 3), (1, 5), (4, 1). It only turns around at the local maxima and minima, and it crosses or touches the x-axis only at the listed points with y = 0.
stops.coldA: Domain \([-7, 6)\). Range \([-4, 6)\). The lowest point is \(y = -4\). The graph rises toward \(y = 6\) at the right end, but that dot is open, so 6 is never reached.
stops.solution: Domain: the graph runs from x = -7 (closed dot, included) to x = 6 (open dot, not included): [-7, 6). Range: the lowest y-value is -4 at (-3, -4). The highest y-value is at the open dot (6, 6), which is not included, so the range is [-4, 6).
stops.mistake: Using the highest local maximum (5) for the top of the range instead of the right endpoint, or using a bracket at an open dot.
stops.again: Find the domain and range of \(h\).[[graph:D]]
stops.againA: Domain \((-6, 5]\). Range \((-6, 4]\). The open dot at \((-6, -6)\) is the lowest place, and it is not reached, so the range starts with a parenthesis.
stops.reflect: Why can the top of the range come from an endpoint instead of a peak?

stops.title: Intercepts
stops.target: Find \(x\)-intercepts (where \(y = 0\)) and the \(y\)-intercept (where \(x = 0\)), written as points.
stops.coldPlain: Using the graph of f, find all x-intercepts and the y-intercept, written as points.
stops.graphNote: It is a smooth curve that starts at (-7, 3) with a closed dot and ends at (6, 6) with an open dot. In order, it passes through (-5, 0), (-3, -4), (-1, 0), (0, 3), (1, 5), (4, 1). It only turns around at the local maxima and minima, and it crosses or touches the x-axis only at the listed points with y = 0.
stops.solution: x-intercepts are where the graph meets the x-axis (y = 0): (-5, 0) and (-1, 0). The y-intercept is where it meets the y-axis (x = 0): (0, 3).
stops.mistake: Writing intercepts as single numbers without the 0, or mixing up which axis each one is on.
stops.reflect: Why does every \(x\)-intercept have a \(y\)-coordinate of 0?

stops.title: Increasing and decreasing
stops.target: Give the intervals where a graph rises or falls (reading left to right), using \(x\)-values in open intervals joined with \(\cup\).
stops.cold: Where is \(f\) increasing? Where is it decreasing?[[graph:C]]
stops.coldPlain: Using the graph of f, give the intervals where f is increasing and where it is decreasing.
stops.graphNote: It is a smooth curve that starts at (-7, 3) with a closed dot and ends at (6, 6) with an open dot. In order, it passes through (-5, 0), (-3, -4), (-1, 0), (0, 3), (1, 5), (4, 1). It only turns around at the local maxima and minima, and it crosses or touches the x-axis only at the listed points with y = 0.
stops.coldA: Increasing on \((-3, 1) \cup (4, 6)\). Decreasing on \((-7, -3) \cup (1, 4)\). Use \(x\)-values only, with parentheses.
stops.solution: Read left to right. The graph falls from x = -7 to x = -3, rises from -3 to 1, falls from 1 to 4, and rises from 4 to 6. Increasing: (-3, 1) U (4, 6). Decreasing: (-7, -3) U (1, 4). These are x-values, in open intervals.
stops.mistake: Writing y-values instead of x-values, or reading the graph right to left.
stops.again: Where is \(h\) increasing? Where is it decreasing?[[graph:D]]
stops.againA: Increasing on \((-6, -3) \cup (2, 5)\). Decreasing on \((-3, 2)\). Notice \((2, 5)\) uses a parenthesis at 5 even though that dot is filled: increasing and decreasing intervals always use parentheses in this section and on CheckIt.
stops.reflect: Why do the intervals use \(x\)-values even though "increasing" is about height?

stops.title: Local and global extrema
stops.target: Identify local maxima and minima (turning points, written as points) and the global maximum and minimum (the greatest and least \(y\)-values the graph reaches, written as values, with where they occur). An endpoint is never a local max or min, but a filled endpoint can be global. A global max or min may not exist.
stops.cold: Find all local maxima and minima of \(f\). Then find the global maximum and global minimum, if they exist.[[graph:C]]
stops.coldPlain: Using the graph of f, find all local maxima and minima as points. Then find the global maximum and global minimum values (and where they occur), if they exist.
stops.graphNote: It is a smooth curve that starts at (-7, 3) with a closed dot and ends at (6, 6) with an open dot. In order, it passes through (-5, 0), (-3, -4), (-1, 0), (0, 3), (1, 5), (4, 1). It only turns around at the local maxima and minima, and it crosses or touches the x-axis only at the listed points with y = 0.
stops.coldA: Local max \((1, 5)\). Local mins \((-3, -4)\) and \((4, 1)\). Global min \(-4\), at \((-3, -4)\). No global max: the graph climbs toward \(y = 6\) at the open dot but never reaches it, and every point it does reach has a higher point to its right.
stops.solution: Local max (a peak): (1, 5). Local mins (valleys): (-3, -4) and (4, 1). Global min: the lowest y-value, -4, at (-3, -4). Global max: none. The graph approaches y = 6 at the open dot (6, 6) but never reaches it, so there is no highest point. (1, 5) is only a local max because the graph goes higher near x = 6.
stops.mistake: Calling (1, 5) the global max, writing a local max or min without both coordinates, or giving a global max or min that the graph never reaches.
stops.again: Find all local and global maxima and minima of \(h\).[[graph:D]]
stops.againA: Local max \((-3, 4)\); the global max is 4, there. Local min \((2, -5)\), but it is not the global min: the graph falls toward \(y = -6\) at the open dot \((-6, -6)\) without reaching it, so there is no global minimum.
stops.stretch: In your own words: how can a graph have a local maximum but no global maximum?
stops.stretchA: A local max only has to be higher than the points right around it. A global max has to be the highest point on the whole graph. If the graph keeps rising toward an open dot that is higher than every point it reaches, no point is highest overall.
stops.reflect: What is the difference between a local maximum and a global maximum?

stops.title: Sketch a graph from criteria
stops.target: Sketch a graph that meets a list of criteria, and label how each criterion shows up on it.
stops.cold: Sketch a graph of a function with all of these features: domain \([-6, 6]\); \(y\)-intercept \((0, 2)\); \(x\)-intercepts \((-4, 0)\) and \((-1, 0)\); local min \((-3, -3)\); local max \((1, 4)\); local min \((4, 1)\); increasing on \((-3, 1) \cup (4, 6)\).
stops.coldPlain: Sketch a graph of a function with all of these features: domain [-6, 6]; y-intercept (0, 2); x-intercepts (-4, 0) and (-1, 0); local min (-3, -3); local max (1, 4); local min (4, 1); increasing on (-3, 1) U (4, 6).
stops.note: I drew a sketch on paper. I'll either upload a photo of it or describe it point by point: where it starts (open or closed dot), each place it crosses the x-axis, where it crosses the y-axis, each turning point, and where it ends. Check my sketch against the criteria one at a time, and ask me to explain how each criterion shows up on my graph.
stops.coldA: Answers vary. Here is one possible graph:[[graph:K1]]Plot the required points first, then connect them so the graph only turns at the listed max and min, and crosses the \(x\)-axis only at the listed intercepts. Closed dots at both ends, since the domain uses brackets.
stops.solution: Answers vary. A strategy: plot every required point first: (0, 2), (-4, 0), (-1, 0), (-3, -3), (1, 4), (4, 1). Start at x = -6 above the x-axis (it must come down through (-4, 0) to the min at (-3, -3)). Rise through (-1, 0) and (0, 2) to the max at (1, 4). Fall to the min at (4, 1) without crossing the x-axis. Rise until x = 6. Use closed dots at x = -6 and x = 6 because the domain is [-6, 6]. One valid graph passes through (-6, 3), (-4, 0), (-3, -3), (-1, 0), (0, 2), (1, 4), (4, 1), (6, 5).
stops.mistake: Crossing the x-axis at a place that is not a listed intercept, adding an extra turn, or using open dots when the domain has brackets.
stops.again: Sketch a graph with all of these features: domain \((-5, 5]\); \(y\)-intercept \((0, -2)\); \(x\)-intercepts \((-3, 0)\), \((-1, 0)\), \((3, 0)\); local max \((-2, 3)\); local min \((1, -4)\); increasing on \((-5, -2) \cup (1, 5)\).
stops.againA: Answers vary. Here is one possible graph:[[graph:K2]]Check: open dot at \(x = -5\), closed dot at \(x = 5\), and the graph crosses the \(x\)-axis exactly three times.
stops.reflect: Which point did you plot first, and why?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same two-part format as the FN3 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Sketch from criteria, and read every feature from a graph, the way the FN3 check asks.
stops.cold:
Part A. Sketch a graph with all of these features, and label how each one shows up: domain \((-7, 6]\); \(y\)-intercept \((0, -3)\); \(x\)-intercepts \((-6, 0)\) and \((-3, 0)\); local max \((-5, 4)\); local min \((-1, -5)\); local max \((2, -1)\); decreasing on \((-5, -1) \cup (2, 6)\).

Part B. For the graph of \(g\), find the domain, range, intercepts, local and global maxima and minima, and intervals of increase and decrease.[[graph:E]]
stops.coldPlain: Part A: Sketch a graph with domain (-7, 6]; y-intercept (0, -3); x-intercepts (-6, 0) and (-3, 0); local max (-5, 4); local min (-1, -5); local max (2, -1); decreasing on (-5, -1) U (2, 6). Part B: For the graph of g, find the domain, range, intercepts, local and global maxima and minima, and intervals of increase and decrease.
stops.graphNote: For Part B: It is a smooth curve that starts at (-7, -6) with a filled dot and ends at (6, -1) with a filled dot. In order, it passes through (-6, 0), (-4, 5), (-2, 0), (-1, -3), (0, -2), (1, 0), (2, 3), (3, 0), (4, -4), (5, -3). It only turns around at the local maxima and minima, and it crosses or touches the x-axis only at the listed points with y = 0.
stops.note: For Part A: I drew a sketch on paper. I'll either upload a photo of it or describe it point by point: where it starts (open or closed dot), each place it crosses the x-axis, where it crosses the y-axis, each turning point, and where it ends. Check my sketch against the criteria one at a time, and ask me to explain how each criterion shows up on my graph.
stops.coldA: A. Answers vary. One possible graph (open dot at \(x = -7\), filled dot at \(x = 6\)): [[graph:K3]]B. Domain \([-7, 6]\). Range \([-6, 5]\). \(x\)-intercepts \((-6, 0)\), \((-2, 0)\), \((1, 0)\), \((3, 0)\); \(y\)-intercept \((0, -2)\). Local maxes \((-4, 5)\), \((2, 3)\); local mins \((-1, -3)\), \((4, -4)\). Global max \(5\), at \((-4, 5)\). Global min \(-6\), at the filled left end \((-7, -6)\): an endpoint, so it is global but not a local min. Increasing on \((-7, -4) \cup (-1, 2) \cup (4, 6)\); decreasing on \((-4, -1) \cup (2, 4)\).
stops.solution: Part A: answers vary; one valid graph starts with an open dot at (-7, -3), rises through (-6, 0) to the max at (-5, 4), falls through (-3, 0) to the min at (-1, -5), rises through (0, -3) to the max at (2, -1) without reaching the x-axis, then falls to a filled dot at (6, -4). Part B: Domain [-7, 6] (filled dots at both ends). Range [-6, 5]: the lowest point is the filled left end (-7, -6), lower than the local min (4, -4). x-intercepts (-6, 0), (-2, 0), (1, 0), (3, 0). y-intercept (0, -2). Local maxima (-4, 5) and (2, 3). Local minima (-1, -3) and (4, -4). Global max 5, at (-4, 5). Global min -6, at (-7, -6) (an endpoint, so not a local min). Increasing on (-7, -4) U (-1, 2) U (4, 6). Decreasing on (-4, -1) U (2, 4).
stops.mistake: Calling (4, -4) the global min when a filled end is lower, missing an x-intercept, using y-values for increasing/decreasing intervals, or putting a bracket in an increasing/decreasing interval.
stops.again:
Part A. Sketch a graph with all of these features: domain \((-6, 5]\); \(y\)-intercept \((0, 1)\); \(x\)-intercepts \((-5, 0)\), \((1, 0)\), \((4, 0)\); local max \((-4, 3)\); local min \((3, -2)\); decreasing on \((-4, 3)\).

Part B. For the graph of \(k\), find all the same features as before.[[graph:F]]
stops.againA: A. Answers vary. One possible graph: [[graph:K4]]B. Domain \((-6, 5]\). Range \([-3, 4)\). \(x\)-intercepts \((-5, 0)\), \((-3, 0)\), \((1, 0)\), \((3, 0)\); \(y\)-intercept \((0, 2)\). Local max \((-1, 3)\); local mins \((-4, -1)\), \((2, -3)\). Global min \(-3\), at \((2, -3)\). No global max, because the graph approaches \(y = 4\) at the open dot but never reaches it. Increasing on \((-4, -1) \cup (2, 5)\); decreasing on \((-6, -4) \cup (-1, 2)\).
stops.reflect: Which feature do you want to practice more before the real check?
